evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (interviews, themes, discussion, and all cited background statistics) concerns patients with Long COVID receiving care at a post-COVID recovery clinic; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a qualitative interview study of 21 adults with Long COVID recruited from a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic, conducted in August-September 2022. It describes patients' lived experience of how Long COVID affected their ability to work, including job loss or change, reduced hours, difficulty balancing work with healthcare appointments, loss of income, changes in insurance (higher deductibles, costlier plans), emotional repercussions such as loss of identity and fear of workplace stigma, and barriers to accessing disability benefits or accommodations. The study does not generate its own cost or productivity-loss estimates; its introduction cites several external studies' percentages and a national wage-loss estimate for background context. The authors' own data are entirely qualitative themes and representative quotations, not quantified financial figures.

modeled_issues.issue: Significant activity limitations reported among a sample of individuals with Long COVID (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: a sample of individuals with Long COVID, per cited reference 2 (NCHS Household Pulse Survey) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Disability reported among a sample of individuals with Long COVID (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: a sample of individuals with Long COVID, per cited reference 3 (US nationwide cohort) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Unable to work 6 months after initial COVID-19 infection (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: individuals with Long COVID, international cohort at 7 months post-infection, per cited reference 6 (Davis et al. 2021) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Required a reduced work schedule (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: individuals with Long COVID, international cohort at 7 months post-infection, per cited reference 6 (Davis et al. 2021) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Unable to return to work one year after COVID-19 infection (cited background statistic drawn from workers' compensation claims data, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: New York workers' compensation claimants with Long COVID, per cited reference 7 (New York State Insurance Fund analysis) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Minimum estimated aggregate lost wages attributable to Long COVID in the USA (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: U.S. working-age population with Long COVID, national aggregate, per cited reference 8 (Suran 2023, JAMA)

contextual_issues: Loss of income due to inability to return to work, forced job changes to lower-paying positions, or reduced/overtime hours - described through participant quotes, not quantified in dollar terms by this study.
Changes in insurance coverage (switching to more expensive marketplace plans with less coverage, deductible and out-of-pocket maximum resets) reported as increasing expenses, but not quantified.
Accumulating debt, tapping retirement funds, and selling personal assets described by some participants as consequences of reduced income, not quantified.

Emotional/mental-health repercussions (loss of identity, fear of judgment, stigma, retaliation) linked to employment changes - described qualitatively, not measured with a validated instrument or quantified burden figure.
Family/household-level financial strain implied (e.g., a spouse's insurance change affecting household finances) but not systematically measured or quantified.
Time and energy costs of balancing work with healthcare appointments described as a barrier to care-seeking, not quantified (e.g., no hours or dollar figure attached).
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost figures (clinic visits, therapies, medications) are reported or quantified by this study.
No direct non-medical cost figures (travel, paid help) are reported or quantified.
No quantified per-patient income-loss or productivity-loss figures; only qualitative illustrative quotes.
No caregiver time or caregiving-cost data were collected.
No longitudinal quantitative follow-up; data come from a single round of interviews (Aug-Sept 2022), so sustained or long-term financial consequences cannot be quantified from this document.

No price-year-stamped, study-generated cost estimates exist in this document; the only dollar figure present ($170 billion) is a cited external background estimate, not derived from this study's participants or methodology.
comparison_boundaries: The $170 billion lost-wages estimate (2022, cited ref. 8) is a separate national aggregate from the 22%/45%/18% employment-impact percentages (cited refs. 6 and 7); these come from different populations, time windows, and measurement methods (an international online self-report cohort at 7 months vs. New York workers' compensation claims data at 1 year) and must not be summed, averaged, or treated as a single consistent range.

The 'approximately one-quarter' activity-limitation and 'nearly two-thirds' disability figures (cited refs. 2 and 3) come from a national household survey and a separate nationwide cohort respectively, with different case definitions and sampling frames; these must not be pooled with each other or with the 22%/45%/18% employment figures.

This study's own qualitative sample (21 patients from a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic, which the authors themselves note is enriched for severe and long-duration symptoms) is not representative of the general Long COVID population and must not be combined with any of the cited national statistics as if describing the same population.

None of the cited background statistics share a common price year, cost perspective, or population definition with each other or with this study's qualitative findings; they should be presented as separate, non-poolable background context rather than a single burden estimate.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The cited 18% figure for 'unable to return to work at 1 year' (ref. 7) is drawn from New York State Insurance Fund workers' compensation claims data, an administrative insurance-claims source; such claims-based figures are subject to the same coding-specificity and access-to-filing undercounting mechanisms described for claims/diagnosis-code-derived Long COVID estimates generally.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The $170 billion U.S. national lost-wages estimate for 2022 (cited ref. 8) and the 22%/45%/18% employment-impact percentages (cited refs. 6, 7) are each presented as single pooled national/cohort figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a lack of established clinical practices or objective diagnostic testing for Long COVID, which makes it difficult for patients and providers to document functional limitations when applying for workplace accommodations, and notes that guidance is still needed for providers on screening and treating the mental health consequences of Long COVID-related employment changes.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section states: 'Due to lack of established practices to diagnose Long COVID, it is important to recognize the challenge of applying for work accommodation without objective diagnostic data' and 'guidance is needed to assist healthcare providers in screening for and treating these conditions among patients with Long COVID.'

crosscheck_candidates.label: Minimum estimated aggregate lost wages attributable to Long COVID in the USA
crosscheck_candidates.definition: Minimum estimated lost wages in the USA attributable to reduced work capacity from Long COVID, as cited by the document from an external source (ref. 8, Suran 2023, JAMA)

decision_relevance.summary: This qualitative study gives detailed, patient-voiced illustrations of how Long COVID disrupts employment, income, insurance access, and emotional well-being, which can help healthcare systems, employers, and policy audiences understand the lived mechanisms behind documented employment and wage-loss statistics rather than providing new quantified cost figures itself. Care delivery teams could use the identified themes (financial toxicity, insurance disruption, stigma, accommodation barriers) to design support pathways such as financial navigation, mental health screening, and accommodation-documentation assistance. Patients and advocates could use the thematic findings to validate and articulate their own experiences when seeking support or policy change. Payers and policy audiences should treat this document as qualitative context, not a source of new cost estimates, and should source actual dollar/percentage figures from the primary studies it cites rather than from this paper directly.
use_cases: Healthcare systems and clinicians could use the identified barriers (lack of diagnostic documentation for accommodations, insurance disruption, stigma) to design financial-navigation and workplace-accommodation support programs for Long COVID patients.

Patient advocates could use the qualitative themes (loss of identity, fear of retaliation, insurance cost increases) to contextualize policy discussions about disability recognition and workplace protections for Long COVID, while being clear that the dollar and percentage figures in the simulator originate from the cited external studies, not from this qualitative study's own 21 participants.

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a qualitative interview study of 21 adults with Long COVID recruited from a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic, conducted in August-September 2022. It describes patients' lived experience of how Long COVID affected their ability to work, including job loss or change, reduced hours, difficulty balancing work with healthcare appointments, loss of income, changes in insurance (higher deductibles, costlier plans), emotional repercussions such as loss of identity and fear of workplace stigma, and barriers to accessing disability benefits or accommodations. The study does not generate its own cost or productivity-loss estimates; its introduction cites several external studies' percentages and a national wage-loss estimate for background context. The authors' own data are entirely qualitative themes and representative quotations, not quantified financial figures.

modeled_issues.issue: Significant activity limitations reported among a sample of individuals with Long COVID (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: a sample of individuals with Long COVID, per cited reference 2 (NCHS Household Pulse Survey) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Disability reported among a sample of individuals with Long COVID (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: a sample of individuals with Long COVID, per cited reference 3 (US nationwide cohort) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Unable to work 6 months after initial COVID-19 infection (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: individuals with Long COVID, international cohort at 7 months post-infection, per cited reference 6 (Davis et al. 2021) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Required a reduced work schedule (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: individuals with Long COVID, international cohort at 7 months post-infection, per cited reference 6 (Davis et al. 2021) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Unable to return to work one year after COVID-19 infection (cited background statistic drawn from workers' compensation claims data, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: New York workers' compensation claimants with Long COVID, per cited reference 7 (New York State Insurance Fund analysis) - not this study's 21 participants

modeled_issues.issue: Minimum estimated aggregate lost wages attributable to Long COVID in the USA (cited background statistic, not this study's own data)
modeled_issues.population: U.S. working-age population with Long COVID, national aggregate, per cited reference 8 (Suran 2023, JAMA)

contextual_issues: Loss of income due to inability to return to work, forced job changes to lower-paying positions, or reduced/overtime hours - described through participant quotes, not quantified in dollar terms by this study.
Changes in insurance coverage (switching to more expensive marketplace plans with less coverage, deductible and out-of-pocket maximum resets) reported as increasing expenses, but not quantified.
Accumulating debt, tapping retirement funds, and selling personal assets described by some participants as consequences of reduced income, not quantified.

Emotional/mental-health repercussions (loss of identity, fear of judgment, stigma, retaliation) linked to employment changes - described qualitatively, not measured with a validated instrument or quantified burden figure.
Family/household-level financial strain implied (e.g., a spouse's insurance change affecting household finances) but not systematically measured or quantified.
Time and energy costs of balancing work with healthcare appointments described as a barrier to care-seeking, not quantified (e.g., no hours or dollar figure attached).
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost figures (clinic visits, therapies, medications) are reported or quantified by this study.
No direct non-medical cost figures (travel, paid help) are reported or quantified.
No quantified per-patient income-loss or productivity-loss figures; only qualitative illustrative quotes.
No caregiver time or caregiving-cost data were collected.
No longitudinal quantitative follow-up; data come from a single round of interviews (Aug-Sept 2022), so sustained or long-term financial consequences cannot be quantified from this document.

No price-year-stamped, study-generated cost estimates exist in this document; the only dollar figure present ($170 billion) is a cited external background estimate, not derived from this study's participants or methodology.
comparison_boundaries: The $170 billion lost-wages estimate (2022, cited ref. 8) is a separate national aggregate from the 22%/45%/18% employment-impact percentages (cited refs. 6 and 7); these come from different populations, time windows, and measurement methods (an international online self-report cohort at 7 months vs. New York workers' compensation claims data at 1 year) and must not be summed, averaged, or treated as a single consistent range.

The 'approximately one-quarter' activity-limitation and 'nearly two-thirds' disability figures (cited refs. 2 and 3) come from a national household survey and a separate nationwide cohort respectively, with different case definitions and sampling frames; these must not be pooled with each other or with the 22%/45%/18% employment figures.

This study's own qualitative sample (21 patients from a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic, which the authors themselves note is enriched for severe and long-duration symptoms) is not representative of the general Long COVID population and must not be combined with any of the cited national statistics as if describing the same population.

None of the cited background statistics share a common price year, cost perspective, or population definition with each other or with this study's qualitative findings; they should be presented as separate, non-poolable background context rather than a single burden estimate.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The cited 18% figure for 'unable to return to work at 1 year' (ref. 7) is drawn from New York State Insurance Fund workers' compensation claims data, an administrative insurance-claims source; such claims-based figures are subject to the same coding-specificity and access-to-filing undercounting mechanisms described for claims/diagnosis-code-derived Long COVID estimates generally.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The $170 billion U.S. national lost-wages estimate for 2022 (cited ref. 8) and the 22%/45%/18% employment-impact percentages (cited refs. 6, 7) are each presented as single pooled national/cohort figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a lack of established clinical practices or objective diagnostic testing for Long COVID, which makes it difficult for patients and providers to document functional limitations when applying for workplace accommodations, and notes that guidance is still needed for providers on screening and treating the mental health consequences of Long COVID-related employment changes.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section states: 'Due to lack of established practices to diagnose Long COVID, it is important to recognize the challenge of applying for work accommodation without objective diagnostic data' and 'guidance is needed to assist healthcare providers in screening for and treating these conditions among patients with Long COVID.'

crosscheck_candidates.label: Minimum estimated aggregate lost wages attributable to Long COVID in the USA
crosscheck_candidates.definition: Minimum estimated lost wages in the USA attributable to reduced work capacity from Long COVID, as cited by the document from an external source (ref. 8, Suran 2023, JAMA)

decision_relevance.summary: This qualitative study gives detailed, patient-voiced illustrations of how Long COVID disrupts employment, income, insurance access, and emotional well-being, which can help healthcare systems, employers, and policy audiences understand the lived mechanisms behind documented employment and wage-loss statistics rather than providing new quantified cost figures itself. Care delivery teams could use the identified themes (financial toxicity, insurance disruption, stigma, accommodation barriers) to design support pathways such as financial navigation, mental health screening, and accommodation-documentation assistance. Patients and advocates could use the thematic findings to validate and articulate their own experiences when seeking support or policy change. Payers and policy audiences should treat this document as qualitative context, not a source of new cost estimates, and should source actual dollar/percentage figures from the primary studies it cites rather than from this paper directly.
use_cases: Healthcare systems and clinicians could use the identified barriers (lack of diagnostic documentation for accommodations, insurance disruption, stigma) to design financial-navigation and workplace-accommodation support programs for Long COVID patients.

Patient advocates could use the qualitative themes (loss of identity, fear of retaliation, insurance cost increases) to contextualize policy discussions about disability recognition and workplace protections for Long COVID, while being clear that the dollar and percentage figures in the simulator originate from the cited external studies, not from this qualitative study's own 21 participants.

spec.title: Long COVID and Employment: Cited Background Statistics from a Qualitative Patient-Experience Study
spec.boundary: This simulation represents only the background percentages and the single national dollar figure that this qualitative interview study (21 patients, one post-COVID clinic, Aug-Sept 2022) cites from OTHER external studies for context. It does not represent this study's own data, which are entirely qualitative themes and quotations about job loss, insurance disruption, and emotional impact, with no dollar or productivity figures of its own. The cited figures come from different populations, time windows, and measurement methods and must not be summed, averaged, or pooled into a single burden estimate.

takeaway.patient: This study doesn't produce new dollar figures about Long COVID's financial impact; instead it shares what 21 patients at one post-COVID clinic described about losing hours, changing jobs, facing insurance cost increases, and feeling dismissed or stigmatized at work. The percentages shown here come from other, larger studies cited only for background context (not from these 21 patients), and they describe different groups measured in different ways at different times, so they should be read as separate snapshots rather than one consistent picture of 'the' typical experience.
takeaway.care: Across the 21 interviewed patients, a recurring workflow issue was that Long COVID has no objective diagnostic test, making it hard to document functional limitations for accommodation or disability applications; patients also described insurance disruption, loss of identity, and fear of stigma tied to employment changes. The cited background percentages (ranging from 18% to 66%, depending on the population and outcome measured) suggest potentially large unmet need for structured support pathways, though they come from different studies and should not be pooled into a single site-level rate.
takeaway.policy: This qualitative study does not generate new cost or productivity-loss estimates; its own contribution is descriptive themes from 21 patients. It cites external estimates for background: a national aggregate of at least $170 billion in lost wages in 2022, alongside employment-impact rates ranging from 18% (workers' compensation claims at 1 year) to 66% (disability in a separate nationwide cohort). These come from different populations, time windows, and methods (self-report cohorts vs. administrative claims data) and must be treated as separate, non-poolable background figures, not components of a single burden estimate.

patient: If you're navigating reduced hours or job loss, know that other patients and cited studies describe this as common, not unique to you - these figures can be talking points, not a personal diagnosis, when discussing your situation with an employer or support group.

If you're worried about documenting your limitations for a workplace accommodation request, ask your care team what information they can realistically provide, since this study notes there is no single diagnostic test for Long COVID.

Consider reviewing your health insurance options (for example, at open enrollment) in light of this study's reports that patients often faced higher deductibles or costlier plans after a Long COVID diagnosis.

If job or income changes have affected your mental health, this study describes loss of identity and fear of stigma as common experiences - consider seeking mental health support that specifically addresses these work-related stressors, not only physical symptoms.
care: Consider whether your clinic's current functional-assessment documentation process gives patients enough support when they apply for workplace accommodations, given the lack of an objective Long COVID diagnostic test.

Evaluate whether a referral pathway exists from the clinic to financial counseling, disability-benefits navigation, and mental health screening for employment-related stress, identity loss, and stigma.

Review how often your own patients report insurance plan changes (e.g., higher deductibles) after a Long COVID diagnosis, and consider whether proactive insurance-navigation support belongs in the care pathway.

Use the cited employment-impact statistics only as background context for program planning, not as site-specific rates, since they come from different populations and measurement methods than your own patient population.
policy: Use the cited $170 billion wage-loss figure and employment-impact percentages only as contextual background in policy briefs, with their original source and population clearly cited, rather than as a figure this study itself produced.

Consider that the workers'-compensation-based 18% unable-to-return-to-work figure likely undercounts true inability to work, since it reflects only filed and approved claims, when evaluating disability-benefit policy adequacy.

Note that none of the cited figures have been disaggregated by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; consider prioritizing disaggregated analysis (e.g., via MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS) before using a single pooled rate for targeted policy design.

Consider funding primary, quantified cost-of-illness research specific to Long COVID employment impacts, since this qualitative study and its cited references do not provide a single internally consistent cost estimate.

package.documentation:
## Parameters and Sources

This simulator is based on a qualitative interview study of 21 adults with Long COVID recruited from a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic (interviews conducted August-September 2022). The study's own data are qualitative themes and quotations about employment disruption, insurance changes, and emotional impact; it does not generate its own dollar or percentage burden estimates.

All numeric inputs and outputs here are background statistics the study cites from other sources, not measurements from its own 21 participants:
- Disability prevalence (66%) comes from a separate nationwide cohort (ref. 3).
- The 22% 'unable to work at 6 months' and 45% 'reduced schedule' figures come from an international online self-report cohort at roughly 7 months post-infection (ref. 6, Davis et al. 2021).
- The 18% 'unable to return to work at 1 year' figure comes from New York State Insurance Fund workers' compensation claims data (ref. 7).
- The $170 billion minimum national lost-wages estimate (2022 dollars) comes from Suran 2023, JAMA (ref. 8).

These figures describe different populations, time windows, and measurement methods and must not be summed, averaged, or treated as one consistent range. All ranges beyond the cited default values are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not values specified by the source document.

## Limitations

**Claims-based undercounting:** the 18% workers'-compensation figure reflects only filed and approved claims, so it likely undercounts the true share of Long COVID patients unable to return to work.

**Subgroup disaggregation:** none of the cited figures (the $170 billion aggregate or the 18-66% employment statistics) are broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

**Systemic evidence gap:** the study notes there is no established clinical practice or objective diagnostic test for Long COVID, which makes it difficult for patients and providers to document functional limitations for workplace-accommodation applications, and that guidance is still needed to help providers screen for and treat the mental health consequences of Long COVID-related employment changes.

This document reports no sex- or gender-based findings of its own.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Minimum estimated aggregate lost wages attributable to Long COVID in the USA: 170,000,000,000.00 in 2022 dollars is about 187,013,069,997.10 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
